artworks.title: Hecuba and Polyxena
artworks.description: Oil painting by the French Neoclassicist Merry-Joseph Blondel, now in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art. After the fall of Troy, the aged queen throws a protective arm around her daughter Polyxena, whom the Greeks claimed for sacrifice at the tomb of Achilles.

artworks.title: Hecuba Blinds Polymestor
artworks.description: Oil painting by the Bolognese painter Giuseppe Maria Crespi, in the Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium, Brussels. Hecuba takes her revenge on Polymestor, the Thracian king who murdered her youngest son Polydorus for his gold: with the captive Trojan women she falls upon him and blinds him, a scene told in Euripides' Hecuba and in Ovid's Metamorphoses.

artworks.title: Hecuba Discovering the Body of Her Son Polydorus
artworks.description: Oil painting by the French Neoclassicist Charles Meynier, painted during his Prix de Rome years in Italy and now in the Horvitz Collection. On a stormy shore after Troy's fall, Hecuba stretches toward the washed-up corpse of Polydorus while her companions restrain her — the shock that, in Euripides and Ovid, turns a captive queen toward revenge on Polymestor.

artworks.title: Hecuba with the Bodies of Polyxena and Polydorus at the Tomb of Achilles
artworks.description: Oil painting by the Viennese Biedermeier painter Karl Russ, in the Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna. Hecuba kneels among the corpses of Polyxena and Polydorus at Achilles' tomb — the twin losses that close her house after Troy, the daughter sacrificed to the dead hero and the son murdered for the gold entrusted to Polymestor.

artworks.title: Hecuba Discovering the Body of Her Son Polydorus
artworks.description: Bas-relief by the French sculptor André-Joseph Allar, his first-year envoi from the Villa Medici, now represented by a galvanoplastic bronze in the Musée des Beaux-Arts, Marseille. Hecuba finds Polydorus cast up on the sand — the Ovidian recognition that opens her vengeance cycle, carved by an artist who had just lost a child of his own.

films.title: The Trojan Women
films.description: Katharine Hepburn's Hecuba is Euripides' fallen queen — the mother who watches her children allotted as spoils while Troy smoulders.

films.title: Troy: Fall of a City
films.description: Frances O'Connor's Hecuba holds the Trojan court through the BBC/Netflix siege — queen, mother, and witness to the house's collapse.

films.title: Helen of Troy
films.description: The USA Network miniseries keeps Hecuba beside Priam as Paris returns and the city falls — the queen killed in the sack.

films.title: Helen of Troy
films.description: Wise's epic stations Hecuba in Priam's palace — the Trojan queen watching Helen arrive and the war consume her sons.

music.title: King Priam
music.description: Tippett gives Hecuba a commanding role among the Trojan women — the queen who demands Paris' death and later mourns what that choice cost.

music.title: Les Troyens
music.description: Berlioz opens in Priam's Troy with the royal house under Cassandra's warnings — Hecuba's court on the eve of the horse.

music.title: Troades
music.description: Reimann's German opera sets Euripides' Trojan Women — Hecabe as alto lead among the captive chorus after Troy falls.

popCulture.title: Hecuba (play)
popCulture.creator: Euripides
popCulture.description: Euripides' tragedy keeps the Trojan queen's grief and revenge on every modern stage — Polyxena sacrificed, Polydorus murdered, Hecuba made a dog in some tellings.

popCulture.title: The Trojan Women
popCulture.creator: Euripides
popCulture.description: Hecuba stands at the centre of the captive chorus — the fallen queen as the face of war's aftermath.

popCulture.title: Hecuba
popCulture.description: Priam's wife endures as motherhood ruined by Troy — fifty sons mourned, and a name still synonymous with tragic queenship.

popCulture.title: Hamlet
popCulture.creator: William Shakespeare
popCulture.description: Hamlet's 'What's Hecuba to him, or he to Hecuba' made the queen a byword for performed grief — tears for a stranger that shame real mourning.

popCulture.title: A Thousand Ships
popCulture.creator: Natalie Haynes
popCulture.description: Haynes opens many chapters through Hecabe — the Trojan queen as the frame for the women the epics left in the shadows.

popCulture.title: The Trojan War Will Not Take Place
popCulture.creator: Jean Giraudoux
popCulture.description: Giraudoux's anti-war play keeps Hecuba among the Trojan voices arguing fate and diplomacy — the queen in a twentieth-century Troy.
